
## Binary variability measures

A final extension of this tutorial concerns measures that are specifically tailored to estimate variability in binary data. Most measures discussed earlier are suitable for continuous (e.g., response time) data, but cannot or are limited in their ability to capture dynamics in accuracy data.  


### Overview of variability measures for binary data
| Variability Estimate | Conceptual Strength | Conceptual Limitation | Suits Data Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Binary Autocorrelation** | Easy to compute | Assumes stationarity | Binary (0/1) data |
| **Sequential Error and Correct Dependency** | Easy to compute, standardized | Assumes stationarity | Binary (0/1) data |
| **Binary Mean Square of Successive Differences (binMSSD)** | Easy to compute, standardized | Conflates autocorrelation with innovations and systematic changes | Binary (0/1) data |
| **Windowed Variance** | Easy to compute, standardized | (Arbitrary) window size choice | Binary (0/1) data | 
: Overview of Binary variability estimates, their strengths, limitations, and suitable data types. {#tbl-overview .striped .hover}

We applied a 'standardization' procedure to each measure which allows for inter-measure comparisons of variability in binary data. All measures discussed below (except for the autocorrelation) are reported in standardized estimates. 

With very large datasets, the computation of these measures can take some time (it isn't "instant," so to speak), because we need to calculate the minimum, maximum, predicted value, etc., for each standardized value. In other words, the standardization procedure slightly increases the computation time.

First we load the required R packages and simulate two datasets: (1) a random simulated and (2) a more realistic binary time-series reflecting more common dynamics. 

#### Set up

##### Load R packages

```{r}
#| label: bivar-source
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: true

## load packages
library(psych)
library(stats)
library(ggplot2)
library(reshape2)

source("PlotMeasures_Function.R") #required for some plotting functions
source("BinVar_Functions.R") #same functions as illustrated in the code blocks below

# For the MSSD, sequential streakiness, and windowed SD, a "standardization procedure" is performed. The functions will output the standardized value by default; it is also possible to specify that you want the "raw" or partly standardized values (see the Bivar_Functions.R script for more information). The functions accept data frames with a time series per row as input. The output is a vector or a data frame with values.

```


##### Two simulated data
Here, we simulate two data sets to illustrate the behaviour of the measures: 
the first data set consists of fully random time series, which is useful for 
checking the successful standardization of the measures:

```{r}
#| label: random-simulation
#| code-fold: false

set.seed(1108)

# create a probabilities matrix with proportions 0 to 1 (101 in total)
probs = matrix(nrow = 101, ncol = 100)
probs[1,]   = rep(0, 100)
probs[101,] = rep(1, 100)
for (p in 1:99) {probs[p+1,] = c(rep(1, p), rep(0, (100-p)))}

# sample each probabilities row 1000 times
# this ensures exactly the same number of time series per proportion correct
# (as opposed to probabilistic sampling)
ran_simdat = matrix(nrow = 101000, ncol = 100)
for (row in 1:nrow(ran_simdat)) {
  ind = rep(1:101, 1000)
  ran_simdat[row,] = sample(probs[ind[row],])
}

# create vector with proportions correct
ran_p = rowMeans(ran_simdat)
```

The second simulated data set aims to integrate some more realistic dynamics 
in the data, to show which types of dynamics are captured by the binary 
variability measures. In order to do this, we first create centered continuous 
time series with different means, autocorrelations, and (polynomial or linear) 
trends. Next, we dichotomize the time series.

```{r}
#| label: real-simulation
#| code-fold: false

# set seed
set.seed(1108)

# generate range of means
p_means = seq(.30, .90, length.out = 100)
z_means = qnorm(p_means)
z_means_input = rep(z_means, 100)

# generate range of autocorrelations
acs = seq(-.30, .90, length.out = 100)
acs_input = rep(acs, 100)

# simulate time series
cont_simdat = matrix(nrow = 10000, ncol = 100)
for (row in 1:10000) {cont_simdat[row,] <- 
  suppressWarnings(arima.sim(list(ar = acs_input[row], ma = 0), n = 100) + 
  z_means_input[row])}

# generate range of linear trends
lins =  seq(-.005, .005, length.out = 100)
lins_input = rep(lins, 40)

# generate range of quadratic trends
quads = seq(-.0005, .0005, length.out = 100)
quads_input = rep(quads, 30)

# generate range of cubic trends
cubics = seq(-.00005, .00005, length.out = 100)
cubics_input = rep(cubics, 30)

# create centered time variable
t   <- 1:100
t_c <- t - mean(t)

# create trend matrix and add linear, quadratic, and cubic trends
trend_simdat = matrix(nrow = 10000, ncol = 100)
trend_simdat[1:4000,] = cont_simdat[1:4000,] + outer(lins_input, t_c)      
trend_simdat[4001:7000,] = cont_simdat[4001:7000,] + outer(quads_input, t_c^2)   
trend_simdat[7001:10000,] = cont_simdat[7001:10000,] + outer(cubics_input, t_c^3)   

# dichotomize
real_simdat = ifelse(trend_simdat<0, 0, 1)
```


##### Binary autocorrelation

Contrary to the autocorrelation in continuous data, the autocorrelation in binary data indicates the degree to which (in-)correct responses are to be followed by another (in-)correct response. 

The binary autocorrelation is defined as: 

$$
\text{binAC}_{\text{raw}} = \text{cor}(y_t, y_{t-k})
$$

and is a priori not 'contaminated' through mean-dependency, making it the only measure where the raw estimate can be used [Schmiedek et al., (2020)](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.9290).

The autocorrelation is essentially a correlation of a time series with 
its lagged counterpart. Say we have the following binary time series:

$$ts = \lbrace 1,1,1,0,1,0,0,1,1,0 \rbrace$$

We first have to center the time series, i.e. subtract its mean (which is .6):

$$ts_c = \lbrace .4, .4, .4, -.6, .4, -.6, -.6, .4, .4, -.6 \rbrace$$

Next, we can construct a "main" time series and a lagged counterpart. 
For an autocorrelation with lag $k = 1$, and the length of the full 
time series $T = 10$, we take $ts_c[1:(T-k)]$ as the main time series, 
and $ts_c[(1+k):T]$ as the lagged time series:

$$ts_{\text{main}} = ts_c[1:9] = \lbrace .4, .4, .4, -.6, .4, -.6, -.6, .4, .4 \rbrace$$

$$ts_{\text{lag}} = ts_c[2:10] = \lbrace .4, .4, -.6, .4, -.6, -.6, .4, .4, -.6 \rbrace$$

We can now compute the covariance of these two time series, and divide 
it by the variance of the full time series. Note that this is the 
standard procedure for computing autocorrelations, which diverges from 
that of standard correlations:

$$\text{binAC} = \frac{(ts_{\text{main}} \cdot ts_{\text{lag}})/n}{(ts_c)^2/n}$$

###### Function

Click "show" to view the implementation of the binary autocorrelation computation in R

```{r}
#| label: binAC-function
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "show"

binAC = 
  # input time series, specify lag k (optional)
  function(ts, k=1) {
  n = length(ts)
  
  # center ts
  ts_c = ts - mean(ts)
  
  # compute covariance between the main and lagged ts; 
  # note we do not divide the cov and var by n as they cancel each other out 
  cov = sum(ts_c[(1+k):n]*ts_c[1:(n-k)])
  
  # compute variance of the complete ts
  var = sum(ts_c^2)
  
  # compute autocorrelation and return
  AC = cov / (var)
  return(AC)
}
```


#### A working example

Let's compute the binary autocorrelation in our simulated data set. Note that 
the `binAC` function requires a single data row as input, so we write a loop 
to go through the data set and save the results in a vector.

```{r}
#| label: binAC-application
#| code-fold: false
#| fig-keep: all

# compute binAC in random data set
binAC_ran <- vector()
for (row in 1:nrow(ran_simdat)) {binAC_ran[row] <- binAC(ran_simdat[row,], k=1)}

# view distribution, compute mean and correlation with mean proportion correct
hist(binAC_ran)
t.test(binAC_ran, na.rm = T)
cor.test(binAC_ran, ran_p)

# note that the autocorrelations show a slight negative small-sample bias,
# which disappears for longer time series:
long_simdat = matrix(NA, 100, 100000)
for (row in 1:nrow(long_simdat)) {long_simdat[row,] = sample(c(1,0), 1000, replace = T)}
long_binAC_ran <- vector()
for (row in 1:nrow(long_simdat)) {long_binAC_ran[row] <- binAC(long_simdat[row,], k=1)}
mean(long_binAC_ran)

# compute in the realistic data set and plot example trajectories
binAC_real <- vector()
for (row in 1:nrow(real_simdat)) {binAC_real[row] <- binAC(real_simdat[row,])}
plot_meas(real_simdat, binAC_real, "Binary autocorrelation")
```


### Binary Mean Squared Successive Difference

For a time series of length $T$, where $y$ represents the score on trial $t$,
the "raw" binMSSD represents the mean squared difference from trial to trial:

$$\text{binMSSD}_{\text{raw}} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T-1} (y_{t+1} - y_t)^2}{T-1}$$

In order to range-standardize the binMSSD, we have to compute the theoretical 
minimum and maximum value for a given proportion correct. The minimum binMSSD 
value can be quite easily conceived: first, when there are only error and correct 
responses, the binMSSD is 0. For any combination of error and correct responses, 
we only need 1 transition if all correct and error responses are clustered. In 
that case, the minimum binMSSD is computed as follows:

$$\text{binMSSD}_{\text{min}} = \frac{1}{T-1}$$

The reasoning behind the maximum possible binMSSD is somewhat more complex. 
Essentially, we need to compute the maximum number of ups and downs possible 
given the length of the time series and the number of correct and incorrect 
responses. This maximum is greatest when the number of errors and correct 
responses is equal: then the time series can go up and down continuously. In 
other cases, the maximum is limited by the number of error or correct responses, 
depending on which of those two is the lowest.

For example, say we have a time series of 100 trials, with 15 errors. The maximum 
binMSSD time series corresponds to a time series where the 15 errors appear 
isolated, creating $15 \times 2 = 30$ "ups and downs" in the data. So the maximum 
is either 1, or computed as follows:

$$\text{binMSSD}_{\text{max}} = \frac{2 \times \min(n_{\text{correct}}, n_{\text{incorrect}})}{T-1}$$

Now, using the minimum and maximum binMSSD values, we can compute the 
range-standardized binMSSD:

$$\text{binMSSD}_{\text{rs}} = \frac{\text{binMSSD}_{\text{raw}} - \text{binMSSD}_{\text{min}}}{\text{binMSSD}_{\text{max}} - \text{binMSSD}_{\text{min}}}$$

We also have to apply the residualization step, for which we need to compute the 
expected binMSSD value in a random time series. For some time series with a given 
$p$, the probability of a transition from a 0 to a 1 or vice versa is equal to 
$p \cdot (1-p) + (1-p) \cdot p$. The number of expected transitions equals this 
probability times the total number of trials, divided by the number of possible 
transitions, $T-1$. Thus, the expected binMSSD becomes:

$$\text{binMSSD}_{\text{exp}} = \frac{(p \cdot (1-p) + (1-p) \cdot p) \cdot T}{T-1} = \frac{2 \cdot p \cdot (1-p) \cdot T}{T-1}$$

We can now range-standardize the expected binMSSD, and use the expected 
range-standardized binMSSD value to compute a final standardized binMSSD score:

$$\text{binMSSD}_{\text{exp-rs}} = \frac{\text{binMSSD}_{\text{exp}} - \text{binMSSD}_{\text{min}}}{\text{binMSSD}_{\text{max}} - \text{binMSSD}_{\text{min}}}$$


$$\text{binMSSD}_{\text{std}} = \text{binMSSD}_{\text{rs}} - \text{binMSSD}_{\text{exp-rs}}$$

#### Function

Click "show" to view the implementation of the binary binMSSD computation in an R function.

```{r}
#| label: binMSSD-function
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "show"

# Input time series, specify output
# The default output is "standardized"
# Other options for output are: "raw", "rangestd"
binMSSD = function(ts, output="standardized") {
  
  # checks whether the ts includes missing data and returns error message if so
  if (sum(is.na(ts)) > 0) 
  {stop("Data includes missingness; please input a data set without missing values")}
  
  # compute raw binMSSD, 
  binMSSD_raw = mssd(ts)
  
  # return if output="raw"
  if (output == "raw")
  {return(binMSSD_raw)}
  
  # compute n correct, p correct, total n trials, n incorrect
  n_cor = sum(ts)
  n = length(ts)
  p = n_cor/n
  n_err = n - n_cor
  
  # max binMSSD: max number of transitions
  binMSSD_max = min(2*min(n_cor, n_err), (n-1)) / (n-1)
  
  # min binMSSD: either 1 or 0 transitions
  binMSSD_min = ifelse(n_cor < (n-1) & n_cor > 1, 1/(n-1), 0)
  
  # compute binMSSD_rangestd
  binMSSD_rangestd  = (binMSSD_raw - binMSSD_min) / (binMSSD_max - binMSSD_min)
  
  # return if output = "rangestd"
  if (output == "rangestd")
  {return(binMSSD_rangestd)}
  
  # compute expected binMSSD
  exp_binMSSD = 2*var(ts)
  
  # compute rangestandardized expected binMSSD
  binMSSD_rangestd_exp = (exp_binMSSD - binMSSD_min) / (binMSSD_max - binMSSD_min)
  
  # compute standardized binMSSD
  binMSSD_std = binMSSD_rangestd - binMSSD_rangestd_exp 
  return(binMSSD_std)}
```

#### A working example

```{r}
#| label: binMSSD-application
#| code-fold: false
#| fig-keep: all

# compute binMSSD
binMSSD_ran <- vector()
for (row in 1:nrow(ran_simdat)) {binMSSD_ran[row] <- binMSSD(ran_simdat[row,])}

# view distribution and mean
hist(binMSSD_ran)
t.test(binMSSD_ran, na.rm = T)
cor.test(binMSSD_ran, ran_p)

# compute in the realistic data set and plot example trajectories
binMSSD_real <- vector()
for (row in 1:nrow(real_simdat)) {binMSSD_real[row] <- binMSSD(real_simdat[row,])}
plot_meas(real_simdat, binMSSD_real, "Binary MSSD")
```



### Sequential Error and Correct Dependency (SED)

Next to the overall streakiness in a binary time-series (i.e., autocorrelation) one could be interested in the separating the overall autocorrelation into a measure that describes the degree of correct and / or error streakiness.

For instance, correct streakiness could be of interest when studying levels of attentiveness whereas error streakiness could be studied when interested in post error behavior.

The measure reported here is the Range standardized residualized SED and is derived from the following process:

For the raw SED, we compute the probability of an error being followed by 
another error:

$$SED_{\text{raw}} = P(y_t=0 \mid y_{t-1}=0)$$

Next, we compute the extra SED, reflecting the probability of an error 
following an error beyond the baseline probability of an error, $1-p$:

$$SED_{\text{ex}} = SED_{\text{raw}} - (1-p)$$

In order to compute the range-standardized SED, we again need to derive the 
maximum and minimum possible extra SED values. First, a maximum SED is obtained 
when all errors follow each other; in that case, $SED_{\text{raw}} = P(y_t=0 \mid y_{t-1}=0)$ 
simply equals 1, and thus the maximum extra SED is equal to:

$$SED_{\text{ex,max}} = 1 - (1-p)$$

The minimum possible SED is somewhat more complex to derive. In case the number 
of errors does not exceed $\frac{T+1}{2}$, there is enough room for "gaps" in 
between all of the errors, resulting in a minimum SED of 0. When the number of 
errors exceeds this number, there are a number of error trials necessarily 
following each other. In that case, the minimum number of trials following each 
other is $n_{\text{err}} - n_{\text{cor}} - 1$. Here, the minimum extra SED can be computed as:

$$SED_{\text{ex,min}} = \frac{n_{\text{err}} - n_{\text{cor}} - 1}{n_{\text{err}} - 1} - (1-p)$$

Where the $n_{err} - 1$ term turns the number of subsequent trials into a 
proportion of subsequent trials. The $-1$ in all these formulas represents the 
last trial, which does not need a gap because there is no trial following it. 
Now, the range-standardized SED can be computed as follows:

$$SED_{\text{rs}} = \frac{SED_{\text{ex}} - SED_{\text{ex,min}}}{SED_{\text{ex,max}} - SED_{\text{ex,min}}}$$

Finally, we residualize the range-standardized value by subtracting the expected 
range-standardized score, resulting in a standardized SED value:

$$SED_{\text{std}} = SED_{\text{rs}} - \frac{0 - SED_{\text{ex,min}}}{SED_{\text{ex,max}} - SED_{\text{ex,min}}}$$

::: {.callout-note}
The formulas for the correct sequential dependency are the (semantic) contrary of the error version.
:::

#### Function

Click "show" to view the implementation of the SED and SCD computation in an R function.

```{r}
#| label: SED-SCD-functions
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "show"

# Input time series, specify output
# The default output is "standardized"
# Other options for output are: "raw", "extra", "rangestd"
SED <- function(ts, output="standardized") {
  
  # checks whether the ts includes missing data and returns error message if so
  if (sum(is.na(ts)) > 0) 
  {stop("Data includes missingness; please input a data set without missing values")}
  
  # compute n correct, total n trials, p correct,  and n errors
  n_cor = sum(ts)
  n = length(ts)
  p = n_cor / n 
  n_err = n - n_cor
  
  # T/F ts denoting succeeding same trials
  same_next <- ts[-length(ts)] == ts[-1]  
  
  # count nr of succeeding errors
  suc_err <- sum(ts[-length(ts)] == 0 & same_next)
  
  # compute raw SED; returns NA if n errors = 0
  SED_raw <- if (n_err > 0) {suc_err / (n_err-1)} else NA
  if (output=="raw") {return(SED_raw)}
  
  # compute extra SED: probability of succeeding errors beyond base rate
  SED_ex <- SED_raw - (1-p)
  if (output=="extra") {return(SED_ex)}
  
  # compute maximum extra SED
  maxSED_ex = 1 - (1-p)
  
  # compute minimum extra SED
  if (n_err < ((n+1)/2) ) {minSED_ex = 0 - (1-p)}
  minSED_ex = ((n_err - n_cor - 1) / (n_err - 1)) - (1-p)
  
  # compute range-standardized SED
  SED_rangestd = (SED_ex - minSED_ex) / (maxSED_ex - minSED_ex)
  if (output=="rangestd") {return(SED_rangestd)}
  
  #compute standardized SED and return
  SED_std = SED_rangestd - ((0 - minSED_ex) / (maxSED_ex - minSED_ex))
  return(SED_std)} 

# The SCD is exactly the same function, with correct responses replacing errors
SCD <- function(ts, output="standardized") {
  
  # checks whether the ts includes missing data and returns error message if so
  if (sum(is.na(ts)) > 0) 
  {stop("Data includes missingness; please input a data set without missing values")}
  
  # compute n correct, total n trials, p correct,  and n errors
  n_cor = sum(ts)
  n = length(ts)
  p = n_cor / n 
  n_err = n - n_cor
  
  # T/F ts denoting succeeding same trials
  same_next <- ts[-length(ts)] == ts[-1]  
  
  # count nr of succeeding errors
  suc_cor <- sum(ts[-length(ts)] == 1 & same_next)
  
  # compute raw SCD; returns NA if n errors = 0
  SCD_raw <- if (n_cor > 0) {suc_cor / (n_cor-1)} else NA
  if (output=="raw") {return(SCD_raw)}
  
  # compute extra SCD: probability of succeeding errors beyond base rate
  SCD_ex <- SCD_raw - p
  if (output=="extra") {return(SCD_ex)}
  
  # compute maximum extra SCD
  maxSCD_ex = 1 - p
  
  # compute minimum extra SCD
  if (n_cor < ((n+1)/2) ) {minSCD_ex = 0 - p}
  minSCD_ex = ((n_cor - n_err - 1) / (n_cor - 1)) - p
  
  # compute range-standardized SCD
  SCD_rangestd = (SCD_ex - minSCD_ex) / (maxSCD_ex - minSCD_ex)
  if (output=="rangestd") {return(SCD_rangestd)}
  
  #compute standardized SCD and return
  SCD_std = SCD_rangestd - ((0 - minSCD_ex) / (maxSCD_ex - minSCD_ex))
  return(SCD_std)} 

```


#### A working example

```{r}
#| label: SED-application
#| code-fold: false
#| fig-keep: all

# compute SED
SED_ran <- vector()
for (row in 1:nrow(ran_simdat)) {SED_ran[row] <- SED(ran_simdat[row,])}

# view distribution and mean
hist(SED_ran)
t.test(SED_ran, na.rm = T)
cor.test(SED_ran, ran_p)

# compute in the realistic data set and plot example trajectories
SED_real <- vector()
for (row in 1:nrow(real_simdat)) {SED_real[row] <- SED(real_simdat[row,])}
plot_meas(real_simdat, SED_real, "Sequential error dependency")
```

### Windowed Variance

While we cannot compute a meaningful variance over binary data, we can break up 
the time series in a set of windows and compute a variance over the means of 
these windows. Say we have a time series of length $T$, and use a window size 
$w$. We can compute the number of windows of size $w$ that fit into a time 
series of length $T$ using integer division:

$$f = \lfloor T / w \rfloor$$

We only keep the trials that are part of a full window, which means all trials 
in the remainder of the time series are discarded. Next, we can compute a mean 
for each of the $f$ full windows in our time series. The windowed variance is 
computed as the variance of the set of window means:

$$\text{winVar}_{\text{raw}} = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{f} (\bar{y}_{j} - \bar{\bar{y}})^2}{f-1}$$
Where $\bar{\bar{x}}$ represents the mean over the window means, which means it 
does not include the trials in the remainder. We can imagine alternative 
procedures for computing the windowed variance, such as a procedure where the 
remainder trials are counted as an extra remainder window. However, including 
such a remainder window would make the standardization of the measure much more 
complex. This means that, whenever the time series length is not a multiple of 
the window size, some trials will not be included in the computation.

We can residualize the raw windowed variance by subtracting the expected windowed 
variance. We know that in a binary time series with proportion correct $p$, the 
variance is equal to $p \cdot (1-p)$. Now, when we cut up the binary time series 
into windows, we are "tempering" the variance, as each window mean tends towards 
the global mean with increasing window size. We can also understand each window 
as a sample from the full time series, where we are interested in the sampling 
variance across windows. Given that we know the "population variance", i.e. the 
variance of the full time series, the expected variance across windows is equal 
to $\text{Var}(y_{\text{full}}) / w$, which is the variance of the full time series 
divided by the window size.

Now we still need the maximum and minimum possible windowed variances. For the 
maximum variance, we need the contrasts between windows to be as large as 
possible. This comes down to reordering the time series so that the first part 
contains all the 1s, and the second part contains all the 0s. This results in 
at least $f-1$ windows containing either only 1s, or only 0s.

For the minimum variance, we want all window means to be as close together as 
possible. For this, we have to perform integer division on the number of correct 
trials, $k$, and the window size. Say that $k = 83$ and $w = 10$ for a time 
series of length $T = 100$; then $k/w$ results in 8 with a remainder of 3. This 
means we need 3 windows with $8+1=9$ correct trials, and $f-3 = 7$ windows with 
8 correct trials. When the remainder is 0, all windows have an equal amount of 
trials, resulting in a variance of 0.

Finally, we can range-standardize both the raw and the expected windowed variance 
and subtract them, which results in a standardized windowed variance.


#### Function

Click "show" to view the implementation of the windowed variance computation in an R function.

```{r}
#| label: winVar-function
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "show"

# Main function
# Input time series, specify output
# The default output is "standardized"
# Other options for output are: "raw", "range-std"
# main function for computing raw, range-std, and standardized windowed variance
winVar = function(ts, output = "standardized", w = 10) {
  
  # deletes NAs at the end of the ts
  ts <- if (all(is.na(ts))) NA else ts[seq_len(max(which(!is.na(ts))))]
  
  # checks whether the ts include missing data and returns error message if so
  if (sum(is.na(ts)) > 0) 
  {stop("Data includes missingness; please input a data set without missing values")}
  
  # compute number of full windows that fit into the ts, cut off remaining trials
  f = length(ts) %/% w # nr of full windows of length w
  ts_full = ts[1:(w*f)] # ts with full windows
  k = sum(ts_full) # nr of 1s
  n_full = length(ts_full)
  
  # compute raw windowed variance; return if output == "raw"
  raw_winVar = winVar_raw(ts_full, w, f)
  if (output == "raw") {return(raw_winVar)}
  
  # compute predicted variance
  # note: we use var(ts)/w instead of (p* (1-p)/w for consistency)
  pred_Var = var(ts_full) / w
  
  # compute min and max; compute range-standardized measure
  max_var = (winVar_max(ts_full, k, w, f))
  min_var = (winVar_min(ts_full, f, k, w))
  range_var = round(max_var - min_var, digits = 10)
  winVar_std = ((raw_winVar - min_var) / range_var) 
  if (output == "range-std") return(winVar_std)
  
  # compute standardized variance
  winVar_res = winVar_std - ((pred_Var - min_var) / range_var)
  return(winVar_res)
}

# helper function to compute raw windowed variance
winVar_raw = function(ts_full, w, f) {
  
  # create vector for saving window means, compute means for the full windows
  w_means = vector() 
  for (win in 1:f) { ind = (win-1)*w+1
  w_means[win] = mean(ts_full[ind:(ind+w-1)])}
  # compute the variance over the means and return
  raw_var = var(w_means)
  return(raw_var)
}

# helper function for computing the minimum winVar
winVar_min <- function(ts_full, f, k, w) {
  spr = k %/% f
  rem = k %% f
  if (rem == 0) {return(0)}
  else {
    counts = c(rep(spr+1, rem), rep(spr, (f-rem)))
    min_ts = unlist(lapply(counts, function(cn) c(rep(1, cn), rep(0, w - cn))))
    return(winVar_raw(min_ts, w, f))  
  }
}

# helper function for computing the maximum winVar
winVar_max <- function(ts_full, k, w, f) {
  max_ts = c(rep(1,k), rep(0, length(ts_full)-k))
  return(winVar_raw(max_ts, w, f))
}

```

#### A working example

```{r}
#| label: winVar-application
#| code-fold: false
#| fig-keep: all

# compute winVar
winVar_ran <- vector()
for (row in 1:nrow(ran_simdat)) {winVar_ran[row] <- winVar(ran_simdat[row,])}

# remove non-finite values before testing
winVar_ran_clean <- winVar_ran[is.finite(winVar_ran)]
ran_p_clean      <- ran_p[is.finite(winVar_ran)]

# view distribution and mean
ggplot(data.frame(x = winVar_ran_clean), aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 200, fill = "#4C72B0", colour = "white", alpha = .8) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of windowed variance (random data)",
       x = "winVar", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

t.test(winVar_ran_clean)
cor.test(winVar_ran_clean, ran_p_clean)

# note that the t-test and correlation are significant due to a minority of 
# extreme values from time series with very extreme proportions correct. 
# The effect disappears when excluding the most extreme proportions:
sel_p          <- seq(.02, .98, by = .01)
winVar_ran_sel <- winVar_ran_clean[ran_p_clean %in% sel_p]
ran_p_sel      <- ran_p_clean[ran_p_clean %in% sel_p]

ggplot(data.frame(x = winVar_ran_sel), aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "#4C72B0", colour = "white", alpha = .8) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of windowed variance (excluding extreme p)",
       x = "winVar", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

t.test(winVar_ran_sel)
cor.test(winVar_ran_sel, ran_p_sel)
# once the two most extreme proportions correct (.01 and .99) are excluded,
# both the t-test and correlation become non-significant as expected for 
# random data

# compute in the realistic data set and plot example trajectories
winVar_real <- vector()
for (row in 1:nrow(real_simdat)) {winVar_real[row] <- winVar(real_simdat[row,])}
plot_meas(real_simdat, winVar_real, "Windowed variance")
```

Note that the distribution is somewhat skewed. The reason for this is that the 
lower bound is stronger than the upper bound for random data: the expected 
windowed variance for a random time series is closer to the theoretical minimum 
than to the maximum value, which is why the distribution is "cut off" at the 
left end.


The large bar at the left side of the distribution is an artifact resulting from 
extreme proportions correct and limited time series length. Fold out the code 
block below for a more detailed explanation.

```{r}
#| label: winVar-large-bar
#| code-fold: false
#| fig-keep: all

# the large bar of winVar values below -.09 belongs to time series with 
# extreme proportions correct
ggplot(data.frame(x = ran_p[winVar_ran < -.09]), aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#4C72B0", colour = "white", alpha = .8) +
  labs(title = "Proportions correct for winVar < -.09",
       x = "Proportion correct", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

# for p = .50 the distribution shows a similar skew as the full distribution.
# the skew exists because time series can deviate from 0 in the positive 
# direction by extreme clustering of 1s and 0s, while negative deviations 
# are limited because the expected winVar is already close to the theoretical 
# minimum for random data
meas_50 <- winVar_ran[ran_p == .50]
ggplot(data.frame(x = meas_50), aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#4C72B0", colour = "white", alpha = .8) +
  labs(title = "winVar distribution for p = .50",
       x = "winVar", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

# this effect is even stronger for extreme proportions correct: for p = .97,
# there are only 3 possible winVar values depending on whether the three 0s 
# appear in different windows or 2-3 appear in the same window. The resulting 
# large negative mode drives the leftward bar in the full distribution.
meas_97 <- winVar_ran[ran_p == .97]
ggplot(data.frame(x = meas_97), aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#4C72B0", colour = "white", alpha = .8) +
  labs(title = "winVar distribution for p = .97",
       x = "winVar", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```
In order to "compensate" for the small minority of extreme winVar values where 2 or 3 0s appear in the same window, the mode deviates quite strongly from 0 in the negative direction. The large negative bar in the distribution of all values combined is the result of these negative modes.

# Conclusion 

Throughout this tutorial, we hope to have illustrated the breadth of statistical measures, each with different strengths and weaknesses, with which researchers can estimate cognitive variability across different data types. This will help further empirical investigation of cognitive variability across a wide range of contexts, tasks and settings. Depending on the scientific question, cognitive process studied, experimental task design and the type of data collected, researchers can make an informed choice among the available measures

```{r}
  output = "table",
  bib.file = "grateful-refs.bib",
  out.dir = getwd(),
  cite.tidyverse = TRUE,
  include.RStudio = FALSE
)

formattable(
  pkgs,
  table.attr = 'class="table table-striped" style="font-size:13px; font-family:Lato; width:80%"'
)
```
